Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease that can cause dark spots on tomato leaves and fruit.
steps: Remove and safely dispose of heavily affected leaves.
Avoid working with plants when foliage is wet.
Avoid overhead watering and keep foliage as dry as practical.
Maintain good spacing and airflow between plants.
Use only locally registered treatments according to the product label and agricultural guidance.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: A fungal disease that commonly produces dark lesions on tomato leaves.
steps: Remove heavily affected leaves where practical.
Improve airflow around plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Keep the area around plants free from infected plant debris.
Use locally registered fungicide options only according to the product label and agricultural guidance.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A serious disease that can spread rapidly under cool and humid conditions.
steps: Separate or remove severely affected plant material where practical.
Avoid overhead watering.
Improve airflow around plants.
Do not move contaminated plant material between healthy plants.
Seek local agricultural guidance promptly for an appropriate registered treatment.
prevention: Monitor plants frequently during favorable weather conditions.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease that commonly develops under high humidity.
steps: Improve ventilation and airflow.
Reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Remove severely affected leaves.
Avoid unnecessary overhead watering.
Use locally registered treatment options according to agricultural guidance.
prevention: Keep foliage as dry as practical.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A fungal disease that produces small spots on tomato leaves.
steps: Remove severely affected lower leaves where practical.
Remove infected plant debris.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Improve airflow around plants.
Use locally registered fungicide options according to the product label and agricultural guidance.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Spider mites are small pests that can cause leaf stippling, yellowing and webbing.
steps: Inspect the underside of leaves carefully.
Remove severely affected plant material where practical.
Reduce plant stress and maintain appropriate irrigation.
Monitor nearby plants because mites can spread.
Use locally registered pest-control options according to the product label and agricultural guidance.
prevention: Regularly inspect the underside of leaves.
Monitor plants during hot and dry conditions.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease that can cause circular lesions on tomato leaves and fruit.
steps: Remove severely affected leaves where practical.
Improve airflow around plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Remove infected plant debris.
Use locally registered treatment options according to agricultural guidance.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A viral disease commonly associated with whitefly transmission and leaf curling/yellowing.
steps: Inspect nearby plants for similar symptoms.
Remove severely infected plants where appropriate.
Manage the insect vector using locally recommended integrated pest-management practices.
Use healthy planting material.
Seek local agricultural guidance because viral diseases generally cannot be cured by fungicides.
prevention: Control weeds that may support insect vectors.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A viral disease that can cause mosaic patterns, leaf distortion and reduced plant growth.
steps: Remove severely infected plants where appropriate.
Avoid touching healthy plants after handling infected plants without cleaning hands and tools.
Clean tools regularly.
Use healthy planting material.
Seek local agricultural guidance for disease-management practices.
prevention: Avoid spreading plant sap between plants.

Tomato___healthy.description: No disease was detected by the current classification model.
steps: Continue regular crop monitoring.
Maintain appropriate irrigation and nutrition.
Inspect leaves regularly for new symptoms.
Monitor for insects and disease development.
